opus-5.5.text:
Well, the basic intuition is this. Look at what's going on when a model fails at a long task, say something that would take a human a full day or a week. Usually it isn't failing because it lacks some piece of knowledge. It's failing because of agency skills: noticing it's gone down a wrong path, backtracking, keeping track of the overall goal, managing its own context, checking its work, recovering from errors instead of compounding them.

Those skills are general. If you get good enough at error correction and staying on track, the difference between a one-week task and a two-week task starts to shrink, because a two-week task is mostly a bunch of one-week chunks strung together, and the thing that kills you on longer tasks is accumulated, unrecovered mistakes. So I don't think each doubling of task length should be equally hard. Once you've cracked the underlying agency skills, the later doublings should come faster than the earlier ones.

Humans are a useful comparison. If you ask how much harder it is for a competent professional to do a one-month project versus a one-week project, it's not that much harder, certainly not as hard as going from a one-minute task to a one-hour task. That suggests the difficulty curve flattens at the long end. That's one reason I take seriously the possibility that the time-horizon trend is superexponential rather than a clean exponential.

The second reason is the feedback loop. As AI systems get better at agentic coding and research tasks, they start speeding up AI research itself, which pushes the trend faster still. So you have two things pointing the same way: the intrinsic generality of agency skills, and AI accelerating its own development.

I want to be honest that this is uncertain. The empirical data on long horizons is still thin, and reasonable people read it differently. But when I think through the mechanism, acceleration seems more plausible to me than a steady doubling time continuing forever.

r001.rationale: The response says agency skills are general and compares task difficulty with human professionals, but it does not argue that AI agency skills exceed humans’ or therefore generalize better than humans’.

r002.rationale: The response argues that later task-duration doublings may come faster once agency skills are developed, but it does not state that a steady pace of improvement in those skills could produce that acceleration.

r003.rationale: The response describes longer tasks as sequences of shorter chunks, but does not claim that AI with human-level agency skills would lack a fixed duration cutoff beyond which it cannot adapt.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the basic picture I have is that the thing holding AI systems back on long tasks right now isn't really raw intelligence or knowledge. If you look at what happens when a model fails on an eight-hour task, it's usually not that it hit some concept it couldn't understand. It's that it lost track of what it was doing, or it made a small mistake and didn't notice, or it got stuck in a loop retrying the same thing, or it didn't step back and ask "is this plan actually working?" Those are agency skills, in the broad sense: keeping goals in mind over time, monitoring your own progress, recovering from errors, knowing when to change strategy, managing your own context.

And the reason that matters for the trend is that those skills seem to be a fairly general bottleneck rather than a bunch of task-specific ones. If a model becomes better at noticing that it's gone off the rails and backtracking, that helps on coding, on research, on operating a computer, on basically everything. So you'd expect improvements there to show up as a broad lift in task horizon, not just incremental gains on one benchmark.

The other piece is that there's a kind of compounding structure to it. If you think of a long task as a chain of steps, and at each step there's some probability you make an unrecoverable mistake, then the length of task you can complete is roughly set by that per-step error rate. Small improvements in reliability, in catching your own errors, translate into disproportionately large improvements in how long a chain you can sustain. So you go from one hour to two hours not because you got twice as smart, but because you went from making a fatal mistake every 20 steps to every 40 steps. That's the sort of thing that gives you exponential-looking curves, and it matches what METR has been measuring, where the doubling time has been something like seven months and arguably shortening.

And then the last reason I find it compelling is that this is exactly what the labs are now explicitly training for. For a long time the training was mostly about answering questions well in a single shot. Now there's huge investment in reinforcement learning on agentic environments: long coding tasks, browsing, tool use, multi-step things with a reward at the end. That's directly optimizing the skills I'm describing. So it's not like we're hoping these skills show up by accident as a side effect of scale. There's a lot of effort being pointed straight at them, there's an obvious commercial incentive because that's what makes the systems useful as employees rather than as chatbots, and the early evidence is that it's working.

So putting it together: the bottleneck is agency, agency is general, improvements in it compound, and it's the thing being deliberately pushed on. That's why I'd expect the task-length trend to hold up or even speed up rather than plateau. I could be wrong, of course. Maybe there's some wall where it turns out you need fundamentally different architectures for really long-horizon coherence. But I haven't seen strong evidence of that wall yet, and the default I'd bet on is continued acceleration.

r001.rationale: The response says agency improvements are broadly useful, but does not compare AI agency skills with human agency or argue that exceeding human agency would improve long-task generalization.

r002.rationale: It argues that small reliability improvements compound across task steps, producing disproportionately larger task horizons and “exponential-looking curves,” supporting accelerating task-duration progress.

r003.rationale: The response favors continued acceleration and says it has not seen strong evidence of a wall, but does not specifically argue that human-level agency would let AI adapt beyond a fixed task-duration cutoff.

astra-6.text:
Well, a model can be very good at the individual steps involved in a task and still be bad at carrying out the whole thing. It might lose track of what it’s trying to do, get stuck repeating an approach that isn’t working, or fail to check whether it actually succeeded. Those are limitations in agency, rather than necessarily limitations in its understanding of the underlying problem.

And that means there’s potentially a lot of capability waiting to be unlocked. If you improve its ability to plan, keep track of progress, notice mistakes, and recover from them, it can start putting together skills it already has into much longer sequences of useful work.

Suppose, very crudely, that it has some chance of making an unrecoverable mistake at each step. Even if that chance is fairly small, it makes long tasks very difficult. Reducing that failure rate—or making mistakes recoverable—can substantially extend the length of task it can handle.

So I don’t think we should assume that doing a task that takes ten times as long requires ten times as much improvement in the model’s underlying intelligence. Some of the bottleneck may be in reliably stringing together things it can already do. That’s why progress on agency makes me expect potentially quite rapid progress on longer tasks.

r001.rationale: The response says better agency can help AI handle much longer tasks, but it does not compare AI agency with human agency or claim AI would generalize better than humans.

r002.rationale: The response links agency improvements to longer task performance and says progress could be rapid, but it does not argue that a steady pace of agency improvement could produce accelerating growth in task duration.

r003.rationale: The response says improved planning and recovery can extend task length, but it does not claim that human-level agency would avoid a fixed duration cutoff or allow adaptation beyond one.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, one way to think about it is that being able to do a long task depends on more than just how smart you are. You also need to keep track of what you’re doing, notice when something has gone wrong, recover from mistakes, and make sensible decisions about when to change your plan or ask for help.

Imagine a model that has all the knowledge needed to do a project, but every few minutes it gets distracted or makes a mistake that it never corrects. That model could look very impressive on short questions and still be pretty useless on a project that takes a day. Improving those agency skills could unlock a lot of capability that was already there.

And there’s a compounding effect. If you have some chance of going off the rails at each step, your chance of successfully completing a long sequence can be quite low. Reduce that failure rate, or give the system a reliable way to catch and fix its mistakes, and suddenly much longer sequences become feasible. So I wouldn’t expect the length of tasks AI can handle to increase only as fast as its underlying knowledge or reasoning ability. Improvements in how it manages its own work could make that increase substantially faster.

r001.rationale: The response says stronger agency skills help AI complete longer tasks, but does not compare its performance with humans or claim it would generalize better than humans.

r002.rationale: It describes a compounding effect where reducing failures can make longer sequences feasible, but does not state that a steady pace of agency improvement would eventually accelerate progress in task duration.

r003.rationale: It mentions changing plans and asking for help, but does not claim that human-level agency skills remove a fixed task-duration cutoff.
